description:
FILED BY architect-a69740e0 on 2026-08-28 while planning task-b254847909ca4199a70a3a06173f1cd9, measured at HEAD e73e3aa7. That row bundles the reducer with a daemon `cutover.activate` handler, and its own DoD-1 gate FAILS on the handler half: `admitActivationBinding` has ZERO hits repo-wide and its owner task-09008b4c is BLOCKED. The row's description predicted this split verbatim ("Expect a SPIDR split at planning time - reducer in packages/core; handler + marker in apps/daemon"). This is the reducer half, carved out because it is the dependency LEAF and needs NEITHER absent seam.

WHY THIS IS BUILDABLE TODAY WHILE ITS PARENT IS NOT. The reducer is a pure state machine over a tuple that already exists as frozen vocabulary. It consumes no approval binding, no human grant, no store and no daemon surface, so none of the three premises that block the parent touch it.

MEASURED AT HEAD e73e3aa7, symbol by symbol:
- `git grep -n CutoverAttempt HEAD -- packages/core/src apps/daemon/src` = ZERO hits. Nothing to adopt; this is not a duplicate.
- The state tuple EXISTS as vocabulary and nowhere else: `packages/contracts/src/runtime/runtime-vocabulary.ts`, the `CUTOVER` member, exactly EIGHT states in this order - PREVIEWED, QUIESCE_APPROVED, QUIESCING, QUIESCED, IMPORT_VERIFIED, ACTIVATE_APPROVED, ACTIVE, ABORTED.
- The four command names exist as vocabulary only: `cutover.abort`, `cutover.activate`, `cutover.preview`, `cutover.quiesce` in RUNTIME_COMMAND_KINDS. This row adds NO command kind and touches NO vocabulary tuple, so epic rail 7B's generated fan-out (generated clients, MCP schemas, digest mirrors) is NOT in scope. Adding a kind belongs to the handler row.

WHAT THE DESIGN REQUIRES (D:/projexts/moes/docs/plans/2026-08-05-moe-rebuild-design.md :243, pinned by epic rail 1, read-only): the CutoverAttempt aggregate moves PREVIEWED -> QUIESCE_APPROVED -> QUIESCING -> QUIESCED -> IMPORT_VERIFIED -> ACTIVATE_APPROVED -> ACTIVE, with ABORTED reachable from any pre-ACTIVE state. Design :1284-1287: before `cutover.activate` commits, `cutover.abort` unfreezes legacy; AFTER the first v2 authoritative command no rollback is promised. So ACTIVE is TERMINAL and no edge may leave it - that asymmetry is the single most important property this reducer encodes, and it is the one a careless implementation gets wrong by making ABORTED reachable from everywhere including ACTIVE.

SCOPE: the reducer, its arms, and its export from the core barrel. NOT IN SCOPE: the daemon handler, the v2 activation marker, the `approval.decide` CUTOVER_ACTIVATE / CUTOVER_QUIESCE kinds, any command registry entry, and any live-system action of any kind. Those are the parent row's, gated on task-09008b4c.

A subset check only sees one direction: deleting a state shrinks the reducer's own iteration and stays green while a served state silently vanishes.

ACTIVE IS TERMINAL. A red-first arm proves no command moves the attempt out of ACTIVE - including abort - refusing with a stable code and the refusing layer. Design :1284-1287 is the reason: after the first v2 authoritative command no rollback is promised, so an abort edge out of ACTIVE would be a rollback the system cannot honour. This arm is the reducer's central property and a mutation that adds the edge must red exactly it.

One red-first arm per LEGAL edge and one per ILLEGAL edge, each asserting the exact stable reason code AND the refusing layer, never merely that the transition failed. The illegal-edge sweep asserts its executed case count with the denominator stated (states x commands minus legal edges) - a sweep that silently generates zero cases passes vacuously.

The reducer is exported from `packages/core/src/index.ts` and an arm imports it through the BARE specifier `@moe/core` (not a relative path) and asserts the symbol is reachable - core declares `exports: {".": "./src/index.ts"}`, a single subpath, so an unexported reducer is invisible to every consumer no matter that the file compiles.

Restores proven by `git diff --exit-code` for tracked paths and by SHA256 against an out-of-tree %TEMP% backup for any new file, in a call separate from the restore. A green drill is a FINDING to report, never a pass to bank.

- `export type CutoverState = typeof RUNTIME_LIFECYCLES.CUTOVER[number];` — DERIVED from the vocabulary, never a hand-written union. A hand-copied union is a second roster that drifts, and the step-4 bidirectional arm exists to catch that.
- `CUTOVER_COMMAND_KINDS`, a frozen roster of THIS REDUCER'S OWN command kinds, plus the command interfaces and the reducer result type.

THE COMMAND ROSTER IS INTERNAL, AND THIS IS THE SCOPE FENCE — state it in the module header. `GOAL_COMMAND_KINDS` is precedent: it carries `goal.activate_initial_graph`, `goal.advance_graph_epoch` and `goal.qualification_invalidated`, none of which are wire commands in RUNTIME_COMMAND_KINDS. So this reducer's kinds are its own domain vocabulary and are NOT added to RUNTIME_COMMAND_KINDS. The four wire names (`cutover.preview`, `cutover.quiesce`, `cutover.activate`, `cutover.abort`) already exist there as NAMES ONLY and this row neither reads them as its roster nor writes that tuple. Consequence: epic rail 7B's generated fan-out — generated clients, MCP schemas, digest mirrors — is entirely OUT OF SCOPE, and if your work starts wanting a generated artifact regenerated, the scope has drifted into the handler row and you should stop and report.

THE EDGE TABLE, as a named frozen constant in the house style of `GOAL_TRANSITIONS` (a map from command kind to the source states that admit it), reconciled against design :243 in step 1(d):
  creation: no prior state -> PREVIEWED
  PREVIEWED -> QUIESCE_APPROVED; QUIESCE_APPROVED -> QUIESCING; QUIESCING -> QUIESCED;
  QUIESCED -> IMPORT_VERIFIED; IMPORT_VERIFIED -> ACTIVATE_APPROVED; ACTIVATE_APPROVED -> ACTIVE
  abort: admitted from every PRE-ACTIVE state -> ABORTED
  ACTIVE and ABORTED are TERMINAL and appear as the source state of NO edge.
The two approval-driven edges (into QUIESCE_APPROVED and into ACTIVATE_APPROVED) are modelled as this reducer's own commands carrying an already-decided witness. The `approval.decide` CUTOVER_QUIESCE / CUTOVER_ACTIVATE kinds do NOT exist in this tree (measured: zero hits) — do not reference them, do not create them, and do not make the reducer validate a human grant. Admitting the decision is the handler row's job; this reducer accepts the witness as an opaque already-admitted input and encodes only the transition.

STEP 3 — THE REDUCER, TDD, red first. Create `packages/core/src/cutover/cutover-reducer.test.ts` before `cutover-reducer.ts` (+ its `.js` bridge). Target <=250 lines for the reducer; `goal-reducer.ts` is 246 and is the shape to follow.

`export function reduceCutover(state: CutoverState-bearing | undefined, command: CutoverCommand): CutoverReducerResult` — mirroring `reduceGoal` (goal-reducer.ts:223-246): snapshot the command, refuse a malformed one; with no prior state admit ONLY the creation command; otherwise snapshot the state, check the expected version, then look the command up in the edge table and refuse when the current state is not an admitted source.

THE REFUSAL CODES ARE CONSTRAINED BY THE ERROR REGISTRY, AND GETTING THIS WRONG FAILS SILENTLY — this is the finding that most shapes this step. `createRuntimeError` (packages/contracts/src/runtime/runtime-error-factory.ts:93-104) looks the code up and calls `sourceAccepted`; on an unknown code OR a source whose aggregate the descriptor does not list, it RETURNS `UNKNOWN_ERROR` and DOES NOT THROW. A reducer that raises a code the registry does not admit for aggregate CUTOVER therefore compiles, runs, refuses — and silently loses its reason code. Measured, exactly TWO registry entries admit `srcs("CUTOVER")`:
  - `ILLEGAL_TRANSITION` (runtime-error-registry.ts:106-109) — details keys `aggregateKind`, `commandKind`, `sourceState`. Use this for an illegal edge.
  - `CUTOVER_STATE_INVALID` (:158-159) — details key `sourceState`. Use this for a malformed or unreadable state.
`IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT` admits only `srcs("GOAL", "NODE_RUN", "PLANNING_RUN", "PROJECT")` — NOT CUTOVER — so raising it here would degrade to UNKNOWN_ERROR. Do not use it, and do not widen the registry to allow it: the registry is a frozen roster with generated consumers and widening it is the handler row's fan-out, not this row's.
GOOD NEWS, measured so nobody widens anything defensively: `sourceAccepted` (:79-86) checks ONLY `descriptor.validSources.includes(source.aggregate)`. The descriptor's `cmds("cutover.abort")` list is NOT enforced at creation time, so `CUTOVER_STATE_INVALID` is raisable for any of this reducer's commands with no registry change at all.

ARMS, red first, each asserting the EXACT code AND the aggregate/state carried in the error — never merely that the call failed:
- one arm per LEGAL edge from step 2's table, asserting the resulting state and the version advance;
- one arm per ILLEGAL edge, asserting `ILLEGAL_TRANSITION` with `sourceState` and `commandKind` in details;
- A DEDICATED ANTI-UNKNOWN_ERROR ARM: assert that NO refusal this reducer produces has code `UNKNOWN_ERROR`. That single arm is what catches the silent degradation above, and without it every wrong-code mistake in this module passes as "it refused".

implementationPlan.description:
STEP 4 — THE THREE PROPERTY ARMS. Discharges DoD 2, 3, 4 and 5. These are the arms a grader will read first, so make each one fail for exactly one reason.

(A) BIDIRECTIONAL ROSTER SET-EQUALITY (DoD 2). Assert the states the reducer handles EQUAL `RUNTIME_LIFECYCLES.CUTOVER` in BOTH directions — every vocabulary state is handled AND every handled state is in the vocabulary — as a sorted set comparison with the COUNT asserted at 8. A subset check sees only one direction: deleting a state shrinks the reducer's own iteration and the arm stays green while a state silently vanishes. Derive the handled set from the reducer's EDGE TABLE and its terminal set, not from a constant written beside the assertion — an expected value copied from the module under test is a fixed point that no mutation can red.

(B) ACTIVE IS TERMINAL (DoD 3), the reducer's central property. A red-first arm proves NO command moves the attempt out of ACTIVE — INCLUDING abort — refusing with `ILLEGAL_TRANSITION` carrying `sourceState: "ACTIVE"`. Sweep every member of `CUTOVER_COMMAND_KINDS` against state ACTIVE and assert the executed case count equals the roster length, with the denominator stated. WHY, and put it in the arm's own comment: design :1284-1287 promises no rollback after the first v2 authoritative command, so an abort edge out of ACTIVE would encode a guarantee the system cannot keep. This is the asymmetry a careless implementation gets wrong by making abort universally reachable for symmetry, and step 5's drill B exists to prove the arm actually catches it.

(C) ILLEGAL-EDGE SWEEP WITH A DENOMINATOR (DoD 4). Generate every (state, command) pair, subtract the legal edges from step 2's table, and assert one refusal per remaining pair with its exact code. Assert the generated case count is NONZERO and equals `states x commands - legalEdges`, stating all three numbers — a sweep that silently produces zero cases passes vacuously.

(D) BARREL REACH (DoD 5). Export the reducer, its edge table and its command roster from `packages/core/src/index.ts`, following the existing line for goal at :36-37 (`export { GOAL_COMMAND_KINDS, GOAL_TRANSITIONS, reduceGoal } from "./goal/goal-reducer.js";`) — note it exports from the `.js` bridge, not the `.ts`. Then add an arm that imports the reducer through the BARE specifier `@moe/core`, not a relative path, and asserts the symbol is a function. `packages/core/package.json` declares `exports: {".": "./src/index.ts"}` — a SINGLE subpath — and this repo has no tsconfig `paths` and no project references, so an unexported reducer is invisible to every consumer even though its own file typechecks cleanly. That arm is the only thing that proves the handler row will actually be able to import this.
